tldr:
Long conversations get summarised, and **summaries blur the facts that matter**: amounts, dates, order numbers, statuses, and what the customer said they need (guide TS 5.1). A **case-facts block** keeps them exact. For it to work, the block must be:

- **Outside the summarised history**, rebuilt into **every** prompt.
- **Structured** (JSON), not a friendly paragraph (docs: structured formats for state data).
- **One record per issue** when the customer raises several (TS 5.1 Skill 2).
- **Kept current**: a new status overwrites the old one.
- **Complete**: it holds what the customer said (“before my wedding on Saturday”), not just what the tools returned.
mentalModel: The summary is the story of the call. The case-facts block is the receipt stapled to the front of the file. Stories get retold vaguely; receipts don't. Keep one receipt per order, cross out the old status when it changes, and write down what the customer asked for — not just what the till printed.
whatItIs:
**In the guide.** TS 5.1 (pp.19–20): Knowledge 1 (what summaries lose), Skill 1 (the block) and Skill 2 (a per-issue layer).
The docs' state-management advice adds: structured formats for state, free text for notes.

**Sub-concepts — each with its picture to remember**

| # | Sub-concept | 🧭 Mental model | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What summaries lose | Stories get retold vaguely; the numbers go first. | ⭐ TS 5.1 · Knowledge 1 |
| 2 | Block outside the summarised history | The receipt is stapled to the front of the file, not folded into the story. | ⭐ TS 5.1 · Skill 1 |
| 3 | In every prompt | The model only sees today's desk; staple the receipt on every time. | ⭐ TS 5.1 · Skill 1 (“included in each prompt”) |
| 4 | Structured, not prose | A receipt has fields; a note says “about eighty quid, soon”. | 📘 docs (state management) |
| 5 | One record per issue | One receipt per order, or the last one overwrites the rest. | ⭐ TS 5.1 · Skill 2 |
| 6 | Kept current | Cross out the old status; don't keep the first one forever. | ⭐ TS 5.1 · Skill 1 (statuses) |
| 7 | Customer-stated expectations | Write down what they asked for, not only what the till printed. | ⭐ TS 5.1 · Knowledge 1 |

**What goes in the block**

| # | Fact | Example | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Amounts | £84.20 | Tool result |
| 2 | Order / case IDs | ORD-5512 | Customer or tool |
| 3 | Dates and deadlines | Friday 14 March | Customer |
| 4 | Statuses | refund approved | Tool result, updated as it changes |
| 5 | Customer-stated expectations | “before my wedding on Saturday 5 April” | Customer |
| 6 | Chit-chat, repeated explanations | — | Leave it to the summary |

**Block vs summary**

| # | Aspect | Summarised history | Case-facts block |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Purpose | The story so far | The exact facts |
| 2 | Format | Prose | Structured (JSON) |
| 3 | Updated by | Re-summarising (loses detail) | Overwriting fields with newer values |
| 4 | Multi-issue | Blended together | One record per issue |
| 5 | Survives compaction | As a vague sentence | Word for word (rebuilt each prompt) |
howItWorks:
1. After every customer message and tool result, **update the block**: set each fact on its issue's record, and let a newer
   value replace an older one.
2. Build every prompt as **block + summary + recent turns**. The block is never itself summarised.
3. Keep it **structured**, and **per issue**, and include what the customer said they need.

grounding.text: Progressive summarisation risks condensing numerical values, percentages, dates and customer-stated expectations into vague summaries.
Extract transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers, statuses) into a persistent case-facts block included in each prompt, outside summarised history.
For multi-issue sessions, extract and persist structured issue data (order IDs, amounts, statuses) into a separate context layer.
Use structured formats such as JSON for state data (like test results or task status), and unstructured text for general progress notes.
grounding.ref: prompting best practices § State management best practices

grounding.text: Compaction replaces older turns with a summary; if the default summary drops something a later turn needs, you can write your own summarisation prompt.
Keeping the block current (overwriting a status when it changes) and including customer-stated expectations are this page's reading of TS 5.1 K1/S1 (statuses; customer-stated expectations).
The events, the summariser, the prose-note writer and the agent's replies are invented to make the effects repeatable; facts arrive pre-extracted so the lab is about the block, not extraction.

examPoints.text: Progressive summarisation turns numbers, percentages, dates and customer-stated expectations into vague summaries.
Extract transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers, statuses) into a persistent case-facts block included in each prompt, outside summarised history.
For multi-issue sessions, persist structured issue data (order IDs, amounts, statuses) in a separate context layer.

variants.label: ✅ ⭐ structured, per issue, kept current, with customer expectations, in every prompt
variants.observe: refund_promise: “You're getting £84.20 back, marked urgent for Friday 14 March.” multi_issue: “For the lamp: £45.00, replacement shipped.” status_change: “Your £199.00 refund is approved.” customer_expectation: an express replacement before the wedding on Saturday 5 April. All of this after every older turn was summarised to a vague sentence.
variants.why: The facts live in their own structured layer that's rebuilt into every prompt, so summarising the history can't blur them.

variants.label: ⭐❌ A — no block: facts only in the summarised history
variants.observe: “Your refund is on its way and should arrive soon.” The amount and date were summarised away.
variants.why: Progressive summarisation keeps the gist and drops numbers, dates and promises.
variants.fix: Keep a case-facts block in every prompt, outside the summarised history.

variants.label: ❌ B — the block written as prose
variants.code:
import json
from utils.casefacts_lab import SCENARIO, prose_note, run_session   # SIMULATED support session


def update_facts(facts, event):
    for f in event["facts"]:                  # amounts, IDs, dates, statuses AND what the customer said they need
        facts.setdefault(f["issue"], {})[f["field"]] = f["value"]   # one record per issue; the newest value wins
    return facts


def build_prompt(facts, summary, recent):
    block = {"role": "system", "content": "CASE FACTS\n" + prose_note(facts)}   # WRONG: a friendly sentence, not data
    return [block] + summary + recent         # in EVERY prompt, outside the summarised history


run_session(update_facts, build_prompt)
variants.observe: The block says the customer “is owed some money back soon”, and the reply is just as vague.
variants.why: The docs: use structured formats (JSON) for state data; free text is for progress notes.
variants.fix: Store the facts as structured data.

variants.label: ⭐❌ C — one flat block for every issue
variants.observe: “For the lamp: £9.99, refund approved” — the mug's values overwrote the lamp's.
variants.why: Multi-issue sessions need structured data per issue, in a separate context layer.
variants.fix: Key the block by order id.

variants.label: ⭐❌ D — facts set once, never updated
variants.observe: “Your £199.00 refund is pending review” — although a later lookup said approved.
variants.why: Statuses are case facts too; the block must reflect the latest value, or it confidently repeats stale data.
variants.fix: Overwrite a field when a newer value arrives.

variants.label: ⭐❌ E — customer-stated expectations left out
variants.observe: “A replacement will arrive in 5–7 working days” — after the customer said the wedding is on Saturday 5 April.
variants.why: The guide names customer-stated expectations among the facts summaries lose. Tool data alone misses them.
variants.fix: Capture what the customer says they need, not only what tools return.

distractors.name: A · No block
distractors.instead: A block in every prompt, outside the summary.

distractors.name: E · Tool data only
distractors.looks: Tools are the source of truth.

questions.q: A support agent summarises the conversation every ten turns and keeps a case-facts block of order numbers and amounts. Early on, a customer explained they are moving house and need the replacement before 3 June. Later, the agent books standard delivery for 8 June. Order numbers and amounts are all handled correctly. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Summarise every 20 turns instead, so that the customer's early statements are summarised less often.
Add customer-stated expectations, such as deadlines, to the case-facts block beside amounts and IDs.
Tell the summariser to always mention any deadline that a customer gives during the conversation.
Ask customers to repeat any deadline just before the agent books a delivery for their order.
questions.explain: Summarisation loses customer-stated expectations along with numbers and dates, so they belong in the persistent block too. A and C only reduce the loss, because the deadline still depends on the summary. D pushes the burden onto the customer.

questions.q: A customer raises a billing dispute and two returns in one conversation. The agent's case-facts block is one flat record, and by the end it quotes the second return's £120.00 refund for the billing dispute. This happens in about 1 in 10 multi-issue conversations. What design keeps the issues apart?
opts: Keep one flat record, but list the most recent issue's values first so that they are easier to find.
Open a separate conversation for each issue automatically, as soon as a new issue is detected.
Replace the facts block with a longer summary that describes each issue in its own paragraph.
Keep structured data for each issue, keyed by its order or case ID, in a separate context layer.
questions.explain: Per-issue records keyed by ID stop one issue's values overwriting another's. A keeps the single record that causes the overwrite. B fragments the customer's experience. C goes back to prose, which is summarised and blurred.

questions.q: A team adds a “case facts” message at the start of each support conversation. Once a conversation is long enough to be summarised, which happens in about 30% of chats, the agent starts giving vague answers about amounts again. What is wrong with the design?
opts: The block is too short, so it should also include the full text of every tool result it records.
The block should be written in prose, so that the summariser treats it as a normal part of the conversation.
The block sits inside the history being summarised; it must sit outside it and go into every prompt.
The block should be added at the end of the conversation, instead of at the start of it.
questions.explain: A case-facts block only protects facts if it sits outside the summarised history and is included in every prompt. A inflates it. B invites the summariser to blur it. D gets summarised too, just later.

questions.q: An agent records a refund as “pending” in its case-facts block. Twenty minutes later a lookup shows the refund approved, but the agent keeps telling the customer it is pending. Audits find this in 6% of conversations where a status changes. What should change?
opts: Remove statuses from the block, and let the agent read them from the conversation history instead.
Add a timestamp to the block, and tell the agent to distrust any value older than ten minutes.
Re-run every lookup before each reply, so that the agent never has to rely on the block for a status.
Update the block whenever a tool result brings a newer value, so it always shows the current status.
questions.explain: The block is only useful if it is current, so each newer value from a tool replaces the old one. A moves the status back into history that gets summarised. B makes the agent doubt facts without refreshing them. C repeats every lookup on every turn.

questions.q: An agent keeps its case state as a paragraph it rewrites itself, such as “customer owed about £80, wants it soon”. After a few rewrites, £84.20 has become “about £80” and “by Friday 14 March” has become “soon”. What does the docs' state-management advice suggest?
opts: Rewrite the paragraph less often, so that there are fewer chances for its values to drift.
Keep state data in a structured format such as JSON; use free text only for progress notes.
Ask the model to be precise with numbers and dates whenever it rewrites the paragraph.
Store the paragraph in a file, so that it survives even when the conversation is summarised.
questions.explain: The docs recommend structured formats such as JSON for state data, and free text for general progress notes. A and C slow the drift down. D persists the paragraph, vague values and all.

questions.q: A support platform switches on automatic compaction for long conversations. The default summary drops the “promised by Friday” commitments customers were given, and 14 customers were let down last month. Besides a case-facts block, what does the compaction documentation offer?
opts: A setting that disables summarisation of assistant messages while keeping all user messages.
A longer compaction threshold, which prevents summaries from ever dropping any commitments.
Writing your own summarisation prompt, so that the summary keeps what later turns need.
A flag that stores every summarised message so that the model can search it later when needed.
questions.explain: Compaction supports a custom summarisation prompt, so you decide what the summary must keep. A, B and D describe options the compaction docs don't offer. A longer threshold only delays the loss.

faq.q: How is this different from D4.7's case-facts tab?
faq.a: D4.7 shows that a block helps, next to other layout techniques. This page is about building the block properly: where it lives, its format, one record per issue, keeping it current, and capturing what the customer said.

faq.q: Where does the block go — system prompt or a message?
faq.a: Anywhere that's rebuilt into every request and never summarised. The lab puts it first, as a system-style message. The guide's requirement is “included in each prompt, outside summarised history”.
No. Compaction is summarisation, and summaries are exactly what blur numbers, dates and promises. The block rides alongside whatever summary you use.
